title: The Hunted
full_review:
As Americans face the reality that the United States may be on the brink of war, the release of the brutal drama "The Hunted" (Paramount) may be ill-timed. The explosive opening scene of an entire Albanian village being slaughtered at the hands of ferocious Serbian soldiers leaves the viewer cold, unable to look away yet repulsed by the brutality.

This scene sets the stage for the rest of the story, in which top Special Forces assassin Aaron Hallam (Benicio Del Toro), who was awarded the Silver Star for killing the Serbian officer who ordered the massacre, snaps after being tormented by nightmares of what he witnessed in the village. In his twisted mind, Aaron decides to protect the innocent by killing those he deems barbarians, starting with two deer hunters using rifles with high-powered military telescopes.

But the killings do not end there. The only man who can track Aaron down and stop him is his mentor and teacher L.T. (Tommy Lee Jones). A retired teacher of warfare ensconced in the snowy wilderness of British Columbia, L.T. wants to forget his past. But his conscience won't let him, so armed only with his tracking skills and the knowledge of how Aaron's mind works, he sets about catching his prey.

Director William Friedkin deftly builds white-knuckle tension in this straightforward story that can only reach one conclusion. And the music by Brian Tyler is brilliant, capitalizing on the fear and dread already felt by the audience. But while the film's carnage is used to justify Aaron's actions, it is excessive to the point of nausea. A little more subtlety and a little less bloodshed would have been more effective.

Jones is refreshingly different in this role. The confident swagger has been replaced with quiet, catlike slink. He plays L.T. as a tentative man, burdened with the realization that although he himself has never killed he has taught dozens -- or more -- how to kill efficiently, gutting their victims' vital organs with small hand-honed machetes. And then there are the letters from Aaron pleading for help as his mental state deteriorates. L.T. has steadfastly ignored them, afraid of being pulled back into a world he doesn't want to step into again.

Unfortunately, Del Toro's character is much less nuanced and the actor does much less with it. It is a physically demanding role, and in this area he acquits himself well. But he fails to dive into Aaron's psyche, making his character one-dimensional when he should have been a complex personality, one who elicits sympathy. Instead Aaron remains at arm's length, just a killing machine.

"The Hunted" is not an easy movie to watch, and is one in which the viewer does not feel a payoff for having sat through so much human destruction.

Because of much savage violence and sporadic rough language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
